Bad: BACK UP THIS DRIVE NOW. Its own firmware says at least one of its health measures has reached the failure limit its maker set.
The details name which one. Spare blocks running out, or reallocation reaching its limit, means the drive is near the end of its life.
Plan to replace the drive, and do not keep the only copy of anything on it.

rules.forecast: A drive that has reached its own failure limit can stop working without further warning.

Bad: BACK UP EVERYTHING ON THIS DRIVE RIGHT NOW, before doing anything else. Copy to another disk or cloud storage first, then continue reading.
The drive predicts its own failure. Replace it — do not wait for it to get worse, and do not trust it with the only copy of anything.
Avoid heavy use (defrag, benchmarks, full scans) until your data is safely copied off.

rules.forecast: Drives that raise this flag frequently fail within weeks. Assume you have days, not months.

Normal: A few sectors have been retired. Back up your files, then re-scan in a week: a stable count is usually fine, a rising count is not.
Bad: BACK UP THIS DRIVE FIRST.
The drive is retiring sectors in quantity — a well-established predictor of failure. Plan to replace it.
Re-scan in a few days: if the number keeps climbing, replace the drive immediately.

rules.forecast: Reallocated-sector growth is one of the strongest failure predictors in large-scale drive studies. Track whether it rises between scans.

Bad: BACK UP THIS DRIVE NOW.
The drive reported errors it could not correct — there is no safe level for this. Replace the drive.
If this drive holds your only copy of anything, copy that data off before any other troubleshooting.

rules.forecast: Drives reporting uncorrectable errors fail at many times the rate of drives that report none.

Normal: Some commands timed out. Check the drive's data and power cables are firmly seated; re-scan afterwards.
Bad: Back up your files, then reseat or replace the drive's SATA data cable and power connector — cabling causes many of these.
If the count still grows on a known-good cable and port, the drive itself is failing.

Normal: A couple of sectors are unstable. Back up now, then re-scan: if the count rises at all, replace the drive.
Bad: BACK UP THIS DRIVE IMMEDIATELY — pending sectors mean data in those sectors may already be unreadable.
Replace the drive. Pending sectors that persist or grow are the single clearest sign a disk is dying.

rules.forecast: Pending-sector counts that grow between scans indicate active media failure — the trend matters more than the number.

Normal: Back up your files and watch this number across scans.
Bad: BACK UP THIS DRIVE FIRST, then replace it — its own background scan is finding sectors it cannot recover.

Normal: Interface errors are usually the CABLE, not the drive. Reseat the SATA data cable at both ends (or try a different USB port/cable for external drives).
This counter never resets and counts the drive's whole life, so a few dozen from a past problem (a loose cable, a hot-plug, an older PC) is harmless — what matters is whether it grows.
Scan again in a week or two with history on: if the number has risen, the app flags it as getting worse. That is the signal to act on.
Bad: Replace the drive's SATA data cable — this is the classic cause and a cheap fix. For USB drives, change the cable and port, and avoid unpowered hubs.
Corrupted transfers can damage files even when the drive itself is healthy, so fix this promptly.

Normal: Warm but acceptable. Improve case airflow if it stays here under light use — cooler drives last longer.
Bad: Too hot for a mechanical drive. Check that case fans work and that the drive has airflow around it; clean out dust.
Sustained high temperature measurably shortens drive life.

Normal: Head parking is accumulating. If this is a laptop drive, reduce aggressive power saving for the disk in the power plan settings.
Bad: The drive is near or past its rated head-park cycles (typically 600,000). Back up and plan replacement.

Normal: The SSD has used most of its rated write endurance. Start planning a replacement; keep backups current.
Bad: The SSD is at or past its rated endurance. Replace it soon — and make sure it is not the only copy of anything important.

rules.forecast: Endurance is consumed by writing. Compare this value across months to estimate how long the drive has left at your usage rate.

Normal: The SSD has used most of its rated write endurance. Plan a replacement and keep backups current.
Bad: The SSD is at or past its rated write endurance. Replace it soon, and do not keep the only copy of anything on it.

rules.forecast: Re-scan monthly: the rate this climbs tells you how many years of writing the drive has left.

Normal: Warm. NVMe SSDs throttle rather than fail, but sustained heat is worth fixing: check airflow, and fit the motherboard's M.2 heatsink if it is unused.
Bad: The drive is hot enough to throttle. Improve airflow, fit the M.2 heatsink, and make sure it is not sitting directly under a hot graphics card.
BACK UP THIS DRIVE NOW — data has already failed to read back correctly.
Replace the drive. Verify your backup opens correctly before trusting it.
BACK UP THIS DRIVE NOW, then replace it — writes are failing, so new data saved here may already be lost.

Normal: This volume is flagged for a file-system check, usually after an unexpected shutdown. Windows will run CHKDSK at the next restart — back up important files first, then restart.
Windows has recorded repairable corruption. From an admin prompt run 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth', then 'sfc /scannow'.
Note those commands repair the system — run them when you can restart afterwards.
Bad: The component store reports non-repairable corruption. Back up your files, then use an in-place repair install of Windows (run setup.exe from a Windows ISO and choose 'Keep personal files and apps').
